utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could already try to find the witness. Meanwhile, Madam Registrar, could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can make use of this time. First, I would like to introduce the Trial Chamber to a member of the trial team, Ms. Julia Lee, who is here with me in court. And the second thing, Your Honour, is that I'm prepared at the end of my examination to make rather detailed submissions about the associated exhibits. I would just ask the Chamber to consider whether it might be a more efficient use of time to postpone that until after the next witness who is here and ready to begin testimony, but I'll be guided by the Chamber. They're somewhat detailed because of their implications for the entire case, but I ask the Chamber to consider when the best time to have those would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that you have put them on paper. Knowing you, Mr. Groome, you usually are well prepared. Is there any way as to have them sent already perhaps to the Defence and to the Chamber what you intend to say and see whether there would be any dispute about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I can't do that right now, but at the first opportunity I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no, it's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let me check with my colleagues whether they would agree with such a procedure as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies, Mr. Harland, for not paying proper attention to you entering the courtroom. Please be seated. I would, first of all, like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Groome will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a small question about the guidance you gave me last night and I was wondering if now would be a good time to put that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Last -- today, as you know, is the anniversary of the fall of Srebrenica and I was contacted last night by a media organisation that asked me after this afternoon whether I'd be willing to give an interview. And they sent three questions and they're actually about Srebrenica as it applies to Syria. And mindful of your guidance, I didn't give a committal reply either way, as I'm not sure whether my testimony will be completed by then. Obviously I hope so, but I seek your guidance on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me, first of all, check with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber instructs you, Mr. Harland, and clarifies its instruction to you that you should not speak with anyone about any matter what is subject of your testimony; subject of your testimony being everything that's found in your statement. So therefore, perhaps it would be wiser at this moment -- although I do understand it cause you some difficulties, but perhaps under the present circumstances that the integrity of these proceedings must prevail above what is perhaps proper attention paying to what has happened in the past.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one more thing. I notice that conversations within teams sometimes go at a certain volume which even goes through my earphones, and that is very likely caused by the fact that if the one speaking is wearing earphones himself at that moment that usually the volume goes up considerably. So could I invite the - and I'm especially at this moment addressing the Defence - could I invite you that if you want to speak to each other that you do it at such a volume level that it does not disturb the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. One more thing. I also had a -- this morning a further reflection on the two questions you put to me, one about cadastral records and the other about water. Neither I think is probably central to the case, and I'm certainly happy to let it pass on but if you're interested I had a further reflection on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first see whether any of the parties wants to re-visit that matter. It could be that further questions are asked in cross-examination. I wouldn't like to anticipate on that. At the end we could still consider whether or not to give you an opportunity to complete your answers in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, if I could begin my questions to you today by drawing your attention to the anti-sniping agreement of the 14th of August, 1994. You discuss it in your statement and the Prosecution will be tendering the document itself, 65 ter 10030. My question to you simply is: Is once that agreement was in place, was there a noticeable diminution of sniping activity into Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for approximately how long did that state last, if you're able?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: For several weeks, but I cannot be more precise after almost 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask now that the court officer bring to our screens 65 ter 10240. And I would ask that we begin by looking at the first page of the document and I will be tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My first question to you, Mr. Harland, when you are able to see the document is can you describe the type of document that we are looking at on our screens?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an UNPROFOR daily sitrep from UNPROFOR headquarters to New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, this document contains a description of a shelling which occurred on this day and which is charged as G(18) in the indictment as well as a summary of all military activity in Sarajevo during this day and the Chamber will be able to read that for themselves. But there is something I want you to clarify which they may have a question about. And if I can draw your attention to the subject line that we can see on the first page and can I ask for your assistance in interpreting the series of numbers and the description that we see in the subject line.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, so it's United Nations peace force headquarters daily situation report, 28 August 1995 from 0001 hour bravo time, which is local time, to 28th of August, 2359 bravo time, which local time one minute before midnight. So it's the 24-hour period of the 28th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, now could I ask that 65 ter 05356 be brought to our screens. It is a document dated the 15th of July, 1995, and authored by Mr. Harland it is entitled: "Sector Sarajevo Weekly Situation Report." And the Prosecution will be tendering this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, once again, when the document is visible on the screen before you, can you please tell us if you recognise it and if you had an opportunity to review it just before testifying?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this one is by me and yes I had an opportunity to review it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could we please advance to page 4 of the original and the middle of page 3 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the second paragraph on this page you describe sporadic bombardment of Sarajevo, and you say: "Apparently in an effort to terrorise the population." And you go on to say that during this period 25 civilians were killed and 98 were wounded. My question to you is: What, if anything, military hostilities were taking place in this week in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is after the Bosnian spring offensive, so it was actually relatively quiet period on the confrontation line but there was significant pressure on the civilian population. So limited conventional military activity around Sarajevo during this week, as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please advance to the last paragraph of page 5 of the original and the last paragraph on page 4 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the last paragraph on this page you write: "The morale of citizens in Bosnia's capital is low. The number of people attempting to desert from the army and to flee the country all together seems to be increasing. There is a general air of fear and disillusionment. Many of UNPROFOR local employees are talking of trying to get out. People talk openly of not being able to stand a fourth winter under siege." My question is the following: Are you able to assist the Chamber in understanding how much of this low morale among the citizens of Sarajevo is due to the eight levers that you describe in your statement and how much is related to other factors unrelated to those eight levers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a difficult question. Obviously there was a cumulative sense of privation and suffering. Even people who had deliberately decided to stay in the city for the first few years were not willing or not able psychologically to cope with the idea of another winter, perhaps without electricity or gas or sufficient amounts of water or food. And the people we interacted -- with us told us that. But clearly it wasn't the only factor. In fact - although General Mladic will be able to clarify more - our assessment was that, in fact, all three sides, the Bosnians, the Serbs, and the Croats, had for different reasons concluded that they should try to end the war in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, would you refrain from telling us who else, including the accused, could give us the information because it's for the parties to decide who they will call as witnesses and for what reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, throughout your statement you talk in some detail about negotiations that you attended in UNPROFOR and different UN officials attended. Did your office ever arrange negotiations directly between the parties; that is to say, between a member of the Bosnian army and the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is there one in particular in relation to Mr. Palic that you personally arranged?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you refer to Colonel Avdo Palic of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you describe what you did to arrange a negotiation with respect to him?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Avdo Palic was the military commander of the Bosnian enclave of Zepa. After Srebrenica fell, the Serb forces began an assault on Zepa. In order to try to minimise the suffering of the civilians, Palic contacted us and said that he would be willing to discuss with the Serbs directly an evacuation of the civilian population of Zepa so that when it came to a final assault on the enclave the civilian casualties would be less. We -- actually, it was not me personally. I sent a colleague of mine, Ed Joseph, to convey that message to the Serb forces assaulting Zepa at that point, and he passed the message to the Serb commander he found, which I believe was General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was -- did your office provide transportation to realise that negotiation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Tolimir said he would welcome that and Colonel Palic should join him at a Serb position immediately above the canyon of Zepa. And so my office put Colonel Palic in one of our vehicles and took him up the winding road to the forward Serb command positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, the Chamber in its recent decision regarding your evidence reminded the Prosecution of the necessity of exploring with you some of the conclusions and opinions in your statement. In paragraph 258 of your statement, you make an assertion that is unequivocal - I don't want to ask you about it. The first sentence of the paragraph, 258, reads as follows: "There was never any doubt whether Mladic had command and control of his military." Are you able to set out in clear, concrete terms for the Chamber the factual basis for such a statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would make two comments. First is about General Mladic's interaction with all the personnel around him. We saw him all the time in the company of General Gvero, General Tolimir, the other, General Milovanovic, and all the more junior officers and the corps commanders, and there was no doubt that they deferred to him on everything and treated him, in fact, with great, extreme respect. More importantly, though, I think our assessment - it wasn't just my assessment, it was a commonly held view among those of us who interacted with him - was that there was a direct connection between General Mladic's statements and results and effects and actions on the ground, down to quite -- from very large matters to quite small matters. So a very trivial thing such as, you know, I myself getting stopped at the Rogatica check-point could eventually be passed all the way up and somebody would say, no, they couldn't allow me or others through or a convoy through until they had personal authorisation from General Mladic to -- and then when it came it would immediately be possible. But, more importantly, large-scale things he could make happen. So you've already asked me at the beginning of this -- yesterday's session about Mount Igman. General Mladic went through in great detail in my presence exactly which positions the Serb forces would be willing to redeploy from from Mount Igman, at exactly what time, to exactly which direction, and they were serious about it because they thought they were going to be bombed by NATO, which they said. And when he ordered it, it happened. He even took several of my colleagues around. He flew in his little small helicopter to the top of Bjelasnica and you could see it happening. Similarly, we also discussed the total exclusion zone that emerged from the cease-fire of February 1994, again when they thought they were going to be bombed by NATO, he gave orders and he told us what the orders were, and our UNMOs in realtime could see the tanks moving, the heavy weapons coming into the collection zones. There was never any doubt in our mind that here was an officer in total command and control of the forces subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You were there in Sarajevo from 1993 until the end of the war. Was there any period during the time you were there that you believed something other than what you've just described?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were periods of tension between the civilian leadership led by Dr. Karadzic and the military structures under the command and control of General Mladic. I never had any doubt that the military structures were effectively under General Mladic's control, but I think there definitely were periods of tension, yes, between the military and the civilian leadership in Pale; particularly, for example, right at the end of the war, July, August, September, October of 1995, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Very practically about your detailed submissions of the associated exhibits, when will we -- when -- I would say especially when will the Defence receive them so they can orient themselves on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the first break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: During the first break. Mr. Lukic, is that then -- you have announced again and again which ones you would want to tender. That means that you should keep in the back of your mind, Mr. Lukic, that they are potentially admitted. And are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am ready, Your Honour, but probably I should receive some guidance regarding the time. I'm interested in how much time do we need for this witness, or we should just go?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there is a lengthy statement of this witness and it comprises a lot; therefore, the Chamber is not intending at this moment to put specific time-limits. Nevertheless, it invites you to be as focused and as efficient as possible and always try to find such a line of questioning that the Chamber understands in which direction we're moving. But could you give us an indication as to how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We calculated and I think nine hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nine hours is a lot, but again --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll try to make it shorter as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will, first of all, observe how you conduct your cross-examination and would advise you to start with the most salient points and not -- of course we leave the cross-examination in your hands, but if at a certain moment we would consider that it has not been of such efficiency that you should be given more time than as you at that point in time say you would need, then at least you've dealt with the most important parts. So try to prioritise as well the matters you would like to raise with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to start from paragraphs 3 and 4 of your statement. Do you have the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can somebody help us so Mr. Harland has a statement with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a hard copy available to Mr. Harland? Mr. Harland, you will find major portions, I don't know whether you're aware of that, blackened out --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraphs 3 and 4, they are not crossed out. We can talk about them. In these paragraphs you talk about your education, and I would like to ask you the following about that: You don't have any military education, training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you don't have any ballistics training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have no medical training?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, may I ask you to give the number of the document? I assume it's P1. We would like to have that displayed on the screen and put the number on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do so. Madam Registrar, can you help us. Is this P1? This gentleman's statement is P1? Can it be put on the ELMO, please -- or actually on the e-court. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be so kind and tell us what were your tasks specifically in Sarajevo at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- for the first period of the war, I was a civil affairs officer in BH command, which was the Sarajevo headquarters of UNPROFOR. And my job was as a political officer to aggregate information from different sources, from contacts with the parties, from our own military contingents and UNMOs and from humanitarian sources and to make analyses and presentations for the UNPROFOR leadership and to participate in organised meetings with the warring factions, both the military and political and humanitarian elements within them and to participate in these and to organise any follow-up to them that might occur. In the final part of the war, I was the head of the civil affairs section for Sector Sarajevo; and then in the very last month or two of the war, I was the political advisor to General Smith, who was the commander of UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement you said that your duties revolved around the political strategy. What did this political strategy encompass, briefly if you can, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, during 1995 there -- after the collapse of the Contact Group plan in 1994 there was an effort, first, to understand what were the war aims of the three major belligerents plus other surrounding states; and to advise the UNPROFOR leadership on how UNPROFOR might best position itself in order to be able to carry out its mandate, either narrowly to assist with delivery of humanitarian aid or, more broadly, to try and bring the conflict to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this include proposals for bombing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now if we can look at paragraph 14, please. There you say that you ensured freedom of movement for civilians. Could civilians freely leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they could not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the area where you lived in Sarajevo, did you see if any Serbs also lived there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in considerable numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were you informed, since you were a civil affairs officer, that Serbs were killed in Sarajevo, Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find out, did you investigate, who killed them, when, and where, and did you report about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We -- when there were casualties, we did attempt to disaggregate the casualty data by the ethnicity of the victims, if possible; and we did attempt to determine the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in these investigations, what did you find? What did you conclude? How many Serbs were killed in Sarajevo during the war, are you able to tell us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- first of all, we certainly did not investigate the death of everybody killed during the period that I was there. It was only a sort of representative sample or we had access to some of the broader data which didn't give particular levels of detail. I think our conclusion was that during the siege roughly 10.000 people were killed all together and roughly 10 per cent of those were Serbs, which was roughly proportional to their share of the population in the area controlled by the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So then you would not agree with me if I were to tell you that more than 5.000 Serbs were killed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw any evidence that affects -- in fact, I would disagree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask whether you are talking about the same Sarajevo. You're talking about Sarajevo. You're talking about the government-controlled area of Sarajevo. Are we talking about the same? Are you putting to this witness that whether he disagrees with the fact that 5.000 people, Serbs, were killed within the area controlled by the government --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So there may be more even in the area outside of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we have verified that. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have information that Serbs in Sarajevo were taken to the front lines to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as UNPROFOR, did you do anything about this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of the issues we protested to the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than protests, did you suggest perhaps any kind of punishment to the Bosnian government -- I would rather refer to them as the Bosniak government. Did you ask for any kind of punitive action against the government?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked -- when there were cases that came to our attention that Serbs had been put into dangerous positions to dig trenches, also we had examples of when Serbs were forced to clear mines by hand from very dangerous areas, such as Stup and Zuc, we lodged a formal protest and we advised them that they were potentially committing war crimes. I remember personally I did this both to General Karavelic and to General Hajrulahovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 19(C) you say: "I was the point of contact with other international and non-governmental organisations operating in Sarajevo, such as UNHCR and the International Committee of the Red Cross." My question is this: Did you receive information from the ICRC about Serb victims, especially for the area that was under the control of the Bosniak government?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on this information, you concluded that it was only 1.000 Serbs who were killed in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say that was the only source of information, no, but that was one of the sources that we would want to consult with.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to look at paragraph 25, please, and there you say: "When I arrived in Sarajevo, the city had been under siege for about a year." The centre of Sarajevo that was held by the Bosniak government at the time, were there Serb settlements around that centre, area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, the population of Serb ethnicity was distributed throughout the area. There was some areas which had higher concentrations of Serbs and there is some like, you know, the old town which had lower concentrations of Serbs. But, in general, they were dispersed throughout the area controlled by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the settlements or neighbourhoods around Sarajevo that were under the control of the Serbs were actually Serb settlements?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The centre of Sarajevo that was under the control of the Bosniaks had a land connection with other areas that were under Bosniak control across from Butmir airport; is that right? And through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- right. The airport was controlled by the United Nations, and then from early 1993 the Bosniaks had completed a tunnel underneath it, so more or less, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know about the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that weapons were being brought into the city through the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if you would kindly look at paragraph 27. You saw a map of Sarajevo yesterday that the Prosecution showed us where lines were marked in red and blue, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude then that fighting was conducted throughout Sarajevo and that the line of separation lay all around Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean that there was fighting around -- along the whole length of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some parts of it were traditionally much more active and some parts were much more quiet, but your general statement is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, we saw on the map that this line of separation was there. Was it 100 metres? Was it 200 metres between the units of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied. In some places that I visited with the French forces, the distance was less than the distance between you and me. So there was a building we called the red building in Grbavica, where one part of the building was controlled by Serb forces and one part of the building was controlled by Bosnian forces. But there were some areas, I would say in the north-east of the city, which were more rural, beyond the city limits, where the distance between the forward positions of the sides might be much greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was fighting in the centre as well, for instance, around Skenderija; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Skenderija itself when I was there. When I was there, Skenderija was well under government control, but there was certainly fighting immediately south of Skenderija, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Grbavica, Vrace, Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Grbavica and Vrace were areas of very intense fighting. Ilijas was outside of the main Sarajevo area and was not a major area of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, there was a separation line running through all of Dobrinja and around the airport; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, a very active line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nedzarici as well, north of the airport, that was under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps while the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina held three sides Alipasino Polje, Mojmilo and Stup, respectively; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a very active part of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I explore, Mr. Lukic. Is there any dispute about what has been the testimony of this witness for the last, well, let's say two pages, that confrontation lines went through these areas, that there was a tunnel, that weapons passed through the tunnel. Is there any dispute about these matters, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it hasn't been established, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, therefore I am a bit surprised that after eight or nine months of negotiations of what could be agreed facts, that there seems to be no problem about it. So therefore we've listened to testimony for at least two pages, if not more, which is apparently not in dispute. The Chamber would very much like the parties to focus on matters which are in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going to continue with this very briefly because we need this in order to move on, that is to say to one of the essential parts of your testimony. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps held Lukavica, that is, 5 to 6 kilometres away from Ilidza, whereas the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in full control in these positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from Mount Igman; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm reminding you of your testimony on the 15th of January, 2007, transcript page 371. This is what you said: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps held Lukavica, that is, 5 to 6 kilometres east of Ilidza, and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled these positions of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from Mount Igman."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would have used the English word "control." I mean, Lukavica and Ilidza were areas under Serb control. I might have suggested that these areas can be fired upon from Bosnian-held high ground on Mount Igman. But the two places you mentioned, Lukavica and Ilidza, were places firmly and safely under the control of Serb forces. But I think there might be an issue with the word "control."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Maybe it's lost in translation.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question in relation to this. To the north-west Sokolj hill, Vogosca, Ilijas, the hill of Zuc, the hill of Hum, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina held under its control the hill of Zuc that was above Vogosca; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move on to paragraph 28. This is what you say: "The entire city was regularly exposed to gun-fire or shelling." That is going to be in dispute here. Who fired at who and from where? That is why I'd like to ask you the following: From the centre of town, that is to say the area that was controlled by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was fire opened at Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had electronic equipment monitoring the shooting and could you establish the direction from which the firing had come?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In most cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, if an anti-aircraft gun was fired and it can fire up to 30 rounds in a very short period of time and also it can be used in infantry fighting, would that be registered as 30 shells or rounds?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a protocol from the agreed among the military observers that multi-fire weapons, rapid-fire weapons, which included those Praga guns and so on, anti-aircraft fire, they would count one burst as one detonation, but one burst might include multiple rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But they can also explode once they hit the target; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The maps which UNPROFOR used each morning to show where heavy rounds had impacted, I believe that they counted from 60-millimetre mortars and above. So Praga gun, anti-aircraft guns, multi-fire weapons were generally excluded; but, you're right, they were in a sort of middle category between light weapons and heavier area weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When there were casualties in the area that was under control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you assumed that the fire had come from the side that was held by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; right? That is what you said in your testimony on page 406 from January 2007.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't and didn't have the capacity to investigate every firing incident, of course, on every victim, but when it was possible to confirm, either from the UNMOs or my military colleagues or directly seeing who was shooting or from mortar detecting radar, then, yes, the overwhelming majority of impacts that landed in the government-controlled part of the city came from the Serb-controlled part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 29 you speak about the predictable regimen of water collection, food collection, and also limited movement. Yesterday you told us - and I'm going to go back to that as well - you spoke about barriers. Is it correct that all of this pertained both to the parts of town that were held by the Bosniak government and army as well as those parts that were held by the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you're not an explosives expert or a military expert for that matter, I am not going to torment you for very long with paragraph 30 [as interpreted], where you said that about 1.000 shells fell every day on the area of the inner city of Sarajevo. Shall we agree that you are not a person that we should discuss this with in detail, a person who kept ledgers, registers, who reported this. You only heard about this at briefings, right? You never went out to see for yourself what had happened except for the individual cases you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true. My job was to aggregate information. Of course all around me the shells were firing, so -- were landing, so I was aware of them to that extent. And when one was particularly interesting, I would go with the UNMO or the battalion teams. But your general characterisation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now paragraph 37, please. You speak about Serb pressure, which meant -- which is shorthand for ratcheting up terror, as you say here. Also, you say that the pressure goes up once peace plans collapse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just for the Chamber to being fully able to follow, you said in your question, page 23, line 23: "I'm not going to torment you very long with paragraph 30, where you said that about 30 shells fell every day -- 1.000."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reading paragraph 30, I do not see that as a statement of the witness, so we are a bit puzzled by --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's clear. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you witness offensives launched by the Bosniak army, offensives that were launched from Sarajevo; and if so, how many did you see for yourself out of the 28?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would sometimes see a part of them. I would see people going to the front line or units being moved or weapons, mortars being moved, or -- because the city was so small, just a few kilometres across, you would also hear and sometimes see the weapons being fired. So, yes, and some of them, you know, like those in the spring of 1995 were basically visible to all residents of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you speak about Igman in this regard on the 15th of January, 2007, transcript page 340, you say that the demilitarised zone in Igman was de facto under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the moment when the demilitarised area was created all the way up until the end of the conflict. And also that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a matter of fact established points of control even behind that. My question: Were offensives often launched against Serb positions from these high altitudes and Serb positions were below?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the Bosnian army did not station heavy weapons that we observed in the demilitarised zone, but it is certainly true that they used it and transited it and launched attacks through it. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we agree then that such a demilitarised zone was a legitimate military objective?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably a better question for you as a lawyer to answer, but I think we can agree that de facto it was not really demilitarised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're discussing the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, tell us what your knowledge is. How many members did the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have within the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can jog your memory. On the 16th of January, 2007, on page 459 you said that the 1st Corps had 30- to 40.000 soldiers within Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it varied over time. I -- it -- during the earlier part of my time, I would guess it had fewer than that and didn't have weapons for all its members. I knew people who shared weapons. It grew over time, but then also over time mobility grew. So they would rotate quite large units out of Sarajevo, for example, in 1995 for combat, for example, in the area of 3rd Corps or even 2nd Corps in the far north. So I'm not sure that I should give a single -- try to give a single number that covers the whole three years that I was there, but some low tens of thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, could we agree that the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had an advantage in terms of personnel levels when compared to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's almost certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the weapons of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were of medium quality, both in terms of quality, maintenance, and replenishment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You promised not to torment me on military issues too much, but that was certainly my amateur assessment that the tanks and the heavy weapons available to the Serb forces were of medium quality and readiness, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also, I'd just like to remind you of your testimony on the 16th of January, 2007, the transcript page is 415, and you say there that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina received equipment and weaponry at the end of 1994 and beginning of 1995, and that at that point in time the Army of Republika Srpska was the weaker side in that area?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is certainly true that the Bosnian army received weapons and uniforms and some training during that 1994 /1995 period. We saw that and we felt a slow shift in the relative balance of power, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, the end of 1994, due to the offensives launched by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you ask for military force to be used against that military component in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, if you want to communicate with counsel, seek an appropriate way rather than talking at a distance. So if you want to address anyone, then -- Mr. Lukic, then apparently Mr. Mladic wants to have a break already -- is that, Mr. Mladic, which -- or you want to consult with counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know maybe -- how much time do we have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We started late, but we usually have a break at 10.30, so if you think this an appropriate moment for a break, then we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would be clever to consult with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we take a break, there is just one brief issue I would like to address to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing to do with the witness. Then I -- and would that not take up much time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think less than a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Less than a minute. Then I suggest we take that. Could you already follow the usher, Mr. Harland. And then, Mr. Groome, please address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, when the Prosecution issued or gave notice of the witnesses it would call, it invited some input from the Defence regarding the approximate time it would think it would to cross-examine the witnesses, and it did not receive any. So I would just renew the request that I think that if Mr. Lukic can provide some estimate, and I accept that it's an estimate and cannot be terribly precise until he hears the witness's testimony, I think we could avoid some unnecessary inconvenience to the witness and also unnecessary expense to the witness. I will go up and speak with the next witness who is here in the building. I would appreciate if there is any guidance the Chamber can give me when it thinks it would want to have him here to receive his evidence so that he can make appropriate plan for the rest of the day or how he uses his time today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think the more important question would be whether he would start his testimony tomorrow, that's -- so for today there's no chance that any next witness would start giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if he -- it looks like he won't start his testimony tomorrow. I think he may wish to return home today to take care of some business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that and perhaps you -- perhaps also use the break and sit with Mr. Lukic, for example, that Mr. Lukic say: I want to raise the existence of a tunnel, any dispute about it? No. Then after the break we'll hear that the parties agree that there was a tunnel under the Butmir airport. That any problem with weapons smuggled through it? No dispute. Okay. That tunnel was used for importing and exporting weapons. Then the next question would perhaps be the size of the troops in Sarajevo and whether there was any change. I think that that would -- Mr. Lukic, these apparently are all facts which are not raised by the Prosecution, most likely because they will not rely on it. But you'll neither confirm, not deny spontaneously because it's -- apparently may not be relevant for your case. But at the same time, if Mr. Lukic apparently wants to raise some issues as the existence of a tunnel, you're not there to deny that that tunnel existed. So, therefore, that can save a lot of time and when I was talking about a focused cross-examination and an efficient cross-examination, I also had in the back of my mind that you try to find out mutually what is in dispute and what is not. I mean, to have a long trial dealing with a lot of matters which apparently are not in dispute between the parties seems not to be the best way of using our time. We take a break, Mr. -- unless there's anything else, we take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. Meanwhile, any discussions between Mr. Lukic and Mr. Groome, any result as far as timing for cross-examination is concerned to be reported?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately not regarding this cross-examination, Your Honour. We did discuss, but we didn't have time to finalise anything of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Under the present circumstances as far as the next witness is concerned, Mr. Groome, it seems to be unrealistic to expect that he could start his testimony any earlier than Friday and I think if that message can be sent to him. I take it that the time at which we'll start on Friday remains the same still, influenced by travel arrangements?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just spoke with the witness. He's willing to take the first plane available so we're looking at that option now. Next week he was fully committed to other things, but he is willing if the Chamber were to be able to say that he would -- his evidence would continue on Monday, he will endeavour in the next hour to rearrange his schedule on Monday and be here for Monday as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will pass that on as well, Your Honour, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, please be seated. The Chamber received a message that it's still a bit unclear what our instructions are in relation to the interview you were asked for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to explain the following: Your testimony is mainly about Sarajevo but not exclusively about Sarajevo. Yesterday questions were asked about matters which were far beyond Sarajevo, so everything that could possibly touch upon what is in your testimony - and that would also be eastern enclaves - you talked about that yesterday - or gas lines - or we do not even know what further in cross-examination could appear, everything that could be linked in any way related -- to be in any way to the subject matter of your testimony in the widest, the broadest sense, you're not allowed to speak about that let alone in public. The Chamber of course therefore asks itself what then remains to be interviewed about. If it is about several years in Bosnia and Herzegovina and not limited to Sarajevo, at the same time if someone wants to interview about and says Syria, were you ever in the Middle East, of course you can answer that question. But if anyone asks you: Syria, do you see any -- could you compare that with the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Then it would immediately stop there because the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the mid -- in the early/mid-1990s is part of your testimony. So we are not the ones who say you could give an interview, yes or no, but we try to clearly explain to you what the instructions are and that is: Do not speak with anyone, either in private or in public, on any matter which could be linked in any way to your testimony or testimony still to be given, which is a rather wide area. What then remains, I leave that in your hands and of the journalist's, but I hope that the instructions are clearer now that we are not in a position to say you shouldn't give an interview. We only can say what you should not talk about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do. Oh, yes, and one more question for you, Mr. Lukic. If you refer to testimony in another case, of course the transcripts are not in evidence for us, would you always refer to the name of the case so that we don't have to find out on what date in what year which case was heard, we know more or less what the point of reference is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Previous transcripts I referred to were from Krajisnik case, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 2007, let me go back in my memory. We'll think about whether that could be correct, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll check it but -- I will check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe you've already identified. It's my understanding that he did not testify in the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe Dragomir Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to avoid to guess on answers of questions, but let's try to stick to the facts. It's an instruction for the future rather than a comment on the past. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 38, please, where you say, among other things, "I came to believe ..." This is your conclusion. It's not the official UNPROFOR position; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure UNPROFOR had a position on it. It was relatively widely shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were eight main levers that Karadzic could use in order to increase the pressure, and then under 2 and 3 you refer to the bombardment of the civilian population and directing sniper fire against the civilian population, did you know at the time the deployment of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the deployment of its cannon, tanks, mortars, snipers in the city in order to be able to say that civilians were fired at?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general we had much better knowledge of where Bosnian government personnel and weapons were because we were also there in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they would move?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about gas, water, electricity cuts only in relation to Sarajevo. Are you familiar of -- with cases when the Muslims knocked these systems out themselves in order to receive international assistance?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And would we agree -- you say that it was a form of pressure. Is that a form of sanctions in order to achieve a political goal?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that this constituted terror. Could it also be a sanction at the same time imposed upon the other warring party in order to weaken its strength?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have had an effect on the military party. I was focusing mainly on its effect on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there an electricity shortage in Republika Srpska also at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there was no gas. There were no neighbourhoods that had a gas system, other than the Dobrinja area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, just a small part under Serb control had gas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary to pay for this gas? It was Russian gas, right, not Serbian gas?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that it was shut off in Mali Zvornik. This is in Serbia, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Sometimes it was shut off in different places, but you're correct, it was sometimes shut off in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If Serbia was instructed, due to unpaid bills, by Russia to shut off the gas -- I mean, would UNPROFOR then sometimes pay for this gas?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I believe some Western countries agreed to pay Russia for the debt on arrears owed on gas to be delivered to Bosnia but not UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this amount was paid?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it correct that the Serbs could have taken Sarajevo militarily?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure as a non-military person I should give my view on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 40 of the statement that we have in front of us you say: "The Serbs could have applied much greater military pressure than they actually did." Had they done that and had they used their military capacity to its full extent and actually directed it against military objectives, they might well have caused the defence of the city to collapse. Would you want to say something different today?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I would say anything different today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your view, what is a more drastic action, the military capture of a city or the imposition of some form of sanction?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the abstract?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] In the abstract, yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if they behave according to the laws and customs of war, then I think they -- the capture of the military objectives and the respect of the population would be less drastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very interesting position, but thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps not without reasons you commented on opinion evidence which was elicited -- was sought to be elicited by the Prosecution, but the Chamber always clearly said: Please, facts, facts, facts, and then we can see whether that opinion would be an opinion which the Chamber could form itself as well on the basis of the factual evidence. I noticed that on legal opinion, on military opinion, and now even again on what is more drastic and -- for you, of course, the same applies as for the Prosecution, that the Chamber is not that much interested in opinion if it has not the facts available and then see whether these facts justify for any of the opinion. That applies to you as well. I would like to remind you of that position of the Chamber, and rightly instigated by you, in relation to this testimony. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 41, the next one, you say that the conflict could best be characterised not as a mid-level conflict but as high-level -- high-intensity gangsterism. This is also an opinion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a characterisation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is that your characterisation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 42, you speak about sniper fire. I would just like to ask you to tell us what was the basis for the difference between sniper fire or just regular rifle fire? How could you know just by the shots that a rifle doesn't have an optical sight?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not easily. If you were shot at close range, it would not always be obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the confrontation line which we more or less partially clarified today, there was firing, as you say, in some areas that was more intense and less intense in other areas. How could you tell the difference if the firing occurred at the front line and that this fire was directed at civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The closer you were to the confrontation line, the more difficult it would be to make a -- to make a distinction. If somebody was, you know, by themselves at some distance from the confrontation line and there was a single shot not in the context of a larger exchange, then that would seem to be more likely to be a sniper incident. But you are correct, when it's close it's not always easy to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In mid-1993 you came to Sarajevo; is that correct? Do you remember the exact date?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. At the time, there was a conflict that broke out between the Croats and the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina around the time that you arrived in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It broke out almost exactly at the time I arrived, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The fighting between Muslims and Croats were primarily conducted in order to capture territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the same time that they were fighting against the Croats, the Muslims were also carrying out offensives in order to join up the Sarajevo-Zenica-Tuzla-and Podrinje areas. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Remember and -- that's correct or you just remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly an ambition they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. And in mid-1993 was there already an assessment then that the Muslims had a sufficient quantity of weapons and ammunition at their disposal to be able to launch a successful offensive against the Croats and the Serbs at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was our view that the Croats who were a much smaller force were surprised by the military capacity of the Bosnian army and that the Bosnian army would not have been able to enjoy the success they did against the Croats, had there also been sustained pressure from the Serb side. And I think, for example, the fighting around Vares and Bugojno was done with Bosnian troops who were actually taken from lines that had been facing the Serbs. So the Bosnians were able to do one or the other, but I think they found it difficult to do both at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we can then conclude that at the time the Serbs were not carrying out any offensive actions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of the Igman offensive, which I think took place during the period of the Bosnian government's fight with the HVO. I don't think there were major Serb offensive military actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now paragraph 48 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, same comments: Opinion, interpretations of facts which have not been presented --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This gentleman should know the fact if Serb were launching any offensives at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking whether the gentleman should know any facts, present the Chamber with facts. The whole issue about so we can -- let me see, whether "they had a sufficient quantity of weapons and ammunition at their disposal to be able to launch a successful offensive against the Croats and the Serbs at the same time." And then we get a lot of an assessment of the military capacity and what they could do, and if they would have done this, that would have been the consequences; all without a factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The whole statement is flooded with data like this. I have to go through the statement. If you want to exclude the statement, I would be happy to sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Point to me where we find the facts which support the opinion which you've asked for. Tell me where we find them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The gentleman refused my question. He said: No, the army wasn't able at that time, the Army of B&H. So obviously he knew that that army wasn't able at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we do not know whether he was right or not. That is his opinion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: His opinion. I mean, what would make us believe that his opinion, not being a military expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and not supported by facts, whether that would -- that's exactly -- you criticised the Prosecution for it. I think we have been very clear: Provide us with the facts rather than with opinion. We do not strike it yet, but more or less ignore it if no underlying facts are presented. The same applies to you. I said it in relation to the previous question. I say it in relation to this question. Again, Mr. Groome is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply to note that it seems that we are concluding upon -- the witness is based as purely on opinion. I ask that he be asked what he based it upon. I believe he does have some information of a concrete nature he could provide the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether he has or not. He certainly has not been asked about it, and that is exactly what we want to prevent to happen. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic. If you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- elicit further --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to show the gentleman the document, but you cut me short. That is the first document I wanted to show him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's number 19198, 65 ter number document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, did you see this document while you were preparing to testify? It was on the list?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't recall that. Since this directive talks about what I have just asked you about -- but if you haven't seen the directive I'm not really going to dwell on it then. You don't recall seeing this document before, do you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. We will move on. In paragraph 48 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just that the witness doesn't speak to this document in his statement. It seems that -- I think the more prudent way to proceed, that if Mr. Lukic would like the witness to look at lengthy documents, it would be fairer to give an opportunity to see them during the break so he can really give an informed decision or informed answer with respect to whether he's seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was - but let me check that - whether he saw it recently during proofing. But, "Did you see this document while you were preparing to testify?" And then he says, "I don't recall that." Therefore I do not know what questions Mr. Lukic is about to ask, if they are limited portions then perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's only the last sentence on the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if the witness could -- if the witness could orient himself what kind of document he's looking at at this moment and then you take him to the portion you would like to ask questions about, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read to you the bit that I wanted to ask you about. It's at the bottom of the page. The sentence begins: [In English] "The Muslim leadership is trying to preserve continuous predominance over Central Bosnia and, if possible, ensure a passage to the sea, the Neretva river delta and to the Sava River the general area of Brcko in this context through offensive operations against both HVO and our forces. They are trying to link up the Tuzla, Zenica, and Sarajevo areas into a whole." [Interpretation] I asked you if you recalled whether this would happen in the field in late June 1993. Perhaps you don't remember if you arrived around that time. [In English] Do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would briefly like to look at paragraph 48. I've been trying to get to it already, several attempts. You talk about the Serbian intention to capture as much territory as possible. Did you see during the time that you were in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the field that the other two belligerents, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the HVO, also tried to capture as much territory as possible in combat?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now please look at paragraphs 50, 51, and 52. There you say that the Serbs intended to capture as much territory as possible and then to return them, and you're talking about Igman here. Did you ever see in practice that the Muslims or the Croats captured something and then subsequently would return it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Serbs were attacking Igman primarily because there were firing points there, firing positions, of the Muslim army; is that correct? I think that we already agreed opposite that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think that's why they took it. I think they took it because it helped them to separate Sarajevo from the main body of Bosnian government-held territory in Eastern Bosnia and they even said that, Dr. Karadzic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Can we now look at document 20884. On the first page here, 3 in the English, at the bottom of the page --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There's no English version in e-court. No translation in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I'll try to read because I do have translation. It's ERN number --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I believe it's not released.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I read one sentence from this document and I will quote the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is a -- if you quote the ERN number and if there is a document to be -- a translation to be released, you may proceed at this moment as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The ERN number of this document is 0401-0692, and the same -- since it's one page it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you then indicate to the witness what kind of a document you are quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is obviously some kind of intercept, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you're supposed to know what you're quoting from, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no title. It looks like intercepted conversation between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I received this from the Prosecution. It's not something we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, anything -- because if we put to the witness a quoted from a document then he's entitled to know what that document purports to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's an intercepted conversation provided by the Government of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It was -- on top of a document it says that it was a conversation between Karadzic and General Milovanovic conducted at 1645 hours on August the 4th, and it was mentioned that Karadzic said: "Please, you shouldn't be in between the hammer and the nail. I am the supreme commander and I am ordering them to withdraw, and tell Mladic to report to me from the airport."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you could Mladic refuse an order like this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, there were certainly periods of tension between them, and this was one of them. They argued like this, in fact, in front of us at the Hotel Panorama, but eventually they both agreed on the redeployment of Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, would there have been air-strikes had the Serbs not withdrawn from Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The agreement was that after the withdrawal of the VRS, these positions should be under UNPROFOR control; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was no agreement to the effect that UNPROFOR would hand these positions over to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Muslim forces, nevertheless, took these positions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct -- or, let me clarify. They certainly dominated. They transited, they put weapons through them, they launched attacks from them. They didn't directly base people there, so -- but your point is generally correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did UNPROFOR do to prevent these actions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we certainly tried to make it logistically difficult and ensure they didn't establish a presence there; and we vigorously protested it, both on the political chain and military chain; and we tried to collect evidence of Bosnian troops crossing the zone, which I saw myself and which I was present at meetings with President Izetbegovic when we showed him the photographs of armed units.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We know that there were no air-strikes that were carried out against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, was this considered as an option because of this violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
